questions.title: Maven POM and Project Structure
questions.question: How does Maven work and what are the key elements of a pom.xml for a Spring Boot project?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- POM: Project Object Model — XML config defining project, dependencies, build lifecycle
- Maven coordinates: groupId + artifactId + version (GAV) uniquely identify any artifact
- Parent POM: inherit config; spring-boot-starter-parent provides defaults for Spring Boot
- Dependency scopes: compile (default), test, runtime, provided
- Maven lifecycle phases: validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy
- maven-wrapper (mvnw): ensures consistent Maven version across team — commit to repo
- Effective POM: what Maven actually uses after inheritance resolution
- BOM (Bill of Materials): import to manage dependency versions without inheritance

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Maven is a build tool that manages the entire lifecycle of a Java project — from downloading dependencies to compiling, testing, packaging, and deploying. Everything is driven by pom.xml, the Project Object Model, which declares the project's identity through groupId, artifactId and version, its dependencies, and how to build it.

Spring Boot projects inherit from spring-boot-starter-parent, which is a carefully curated POM that sets up sensible defaults — Java version, encoding, plugin configuration, and most importantly, a dependency management section with compatible versions for hundreds of libraries. When you add spring-boot-starter-web without a version, Maven resolves the correct compatible version from the parent.

The dependency scope determines when a dependency is on the classpath. Compile is the default — available everywhere. Test is only for test compilation and execution, not packaged into the final JAR. Runtime is needed at runtime but not to compile the application — like a database driver. Provided means the container or runtime provides it, so don't include it in the JAR — like servlet-api when deploying to a server.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Standard Spring Boot pom.xml

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <!-- Inherit Spring Boot defaults: dependency management, plugin config -->
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.2.5</version>
        <relativePath/>
    </parent>

    <!-- Project identity (GAV) -->
    <groupId>com.mycompany</groupId>
    <artifactId>order-service</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <packaging>jar</packaging>

    <properties>
        <java.version>21</java.version>
        <!-- Override any dependency version from parent BOM -->
        <postgresql.version>42.7.3</postgresql.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- Compile scope (default) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
            <!-- No version needed — resolved from parent BOM -->
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
        </dependency>

        <!-- Runtime scope — driver not needed to compile, just to run -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
            <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
            <scope>runtime</scope>
        </dependency>

        <!-- Test scope — only in test classpath -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <!-- Spring Boot plugin: repackage into executable fat JAR -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <configuration>
                    <excludes>
                        <exclude>
                            <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
                            <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
                        </exclude>
                    </excludes>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
```

## Key Maven Commands

```bash
./mvnw clean package          # clean + compile + test + package JAR
./mvnw clean package -DskipTests  # skip tests (not recommended for CI)
./mvnw test                   # run tests only
./mvnw spring-boot:run        # run Spring Boot app directly
./mvnw dependency:tree        # show full dependency tree
./mvnw dependency:analyze     # find unused/undeclared dependencies
./mvnw help:effective-pom     # show final resolved POM
./mvnw versions:display-dependency-updates  # check for newer dependency versions
```

## Dependency Scopes

| Scope | Compile | Test | Runtime | Packaged |
|-------|---------|------|---------|----------|
| compile | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| test | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| runtime | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| provided | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |

questions.title: Maven Lifecycle and Plugins
questions.question: How does the Maven build lifecycle work and what are the most useful plugins for a Java backend?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Default lifecycle phases: validate, compile, test, package, integration-test, verify, install, deploy
- Running a phase runs all previous phases too: mvn package = validate + compile + test + package
- Plugins: maven-compiler-plugin, maven-surefire-plugin (unit tests), maven-failsafe-plugin (integration tests)
- Jacoco: code coverage report and enforcement
- Checkstyle / SpotBugs / PMD: static analysis
- maven-enforcer-plugin: enforce rules (min Java version, dependency conflict rules)
- Flyway Maven plugin: run migrations from command line
- Profile: run different configs for different environments

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Maven's default lifecycle has phases that run in sequence, and each subsequent phase includes all previous ones. When you run mvn package, Maven runs validate, compile, test, and then package. This is why you don't have to separately run compile before test — the lifecycle handles the ordering.

Plugins are how you extend the lifecycle. The maven-surefire-plugin runs unit tests during the test phase. The maven-failsafe-plugin runs integration tests during the integration-test phase — these are intentionally separate because integration tests require an environment and are slower. Jacoco attaches to both to generate coverage reports and can fail the build if coverage drops below a threshold.

The maven-enforcer-plugin is underused but valuable. You can enforce that the project uses at least a specific Maven version, that it uses a specific Java version, that there are no dependency convergence issues where two different dependencies pull in different versions of the same transitive dependency. Making these failures instead of warnings prevents hard-to-diagnose runtime problems.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Plugin Configuration Examples

```xml
<build>
    <plugins>
        <!-- Compiler: Java 21 with explicit annotation processors -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
            <configuration>
                <source>21</source>
                <target>21</target>
                <compilerArgs>
                    <arg>-parameters</arg>  <!-- preserve parameter names for Spring -->
                </compilerArgs>
            </configuration>
        </plugin>

        <!-- Surefire: unit tests (excludes IT) -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
            <configuration>
                <excludes>
                    <exclude>**/*IT.java</exclude>
                    <exclude>**/*IntegrationTest.java</exclude>
                </excludes>
            </configuration>
        </plugin>

        <!-- Failsafe: integration tests during integration-test phase -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
            <executions>
                <execution>
                    <goals>
                        <goal>integration-test</goal>
                        <goal>verify</goal>
                    </goals>
                </execution>
            </executions>
        </plugin>

        <!-- Jacoco: code coverage -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
            <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            <executions>
                <execution>
                    <goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals>
                </execution>
                <execution>
                    <id>report</id>
                    <phase>verify</phase>
                    <goals><goal>report</goal></goals>
                </execution>
                <execution>
                    <id>check</id>
                    <goals><goal>check</goal></goals>
                    <configuration>
                        <rules>
                            <rule>
                                <limits>
                                    <limit>
                                        <counter>LINE</counter>
                                        <value>COVEREDRATIO</value>
                                        <minimum>0.80</minimum>  <!-- 80% coverage required -->
                                    </limit>
                                </limits>
                            </rule>
                        </rules>
                    </configuration>
                </execution>
            </executions>
        </plugin>

        <!-- Enforcer: prevent dependency conflicts and enforce Java version -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-enforcer-plugin</artifactId>
            <executions>
                <execution>
                    <goals><goal>enforce</goal></goals>
                    <configuration>
                        <rules>
                            <requireJavaVersion>
                                <version>[21,)</version>
                            </requireJavaVersion>
                            <requireMavenVersion>
                                <version>[3.9,)</version>
                            </requireMavenVersion>
                            <dependencyConvergence/>
                        </rules>
                    </configuration>
                </execution>
            </executions>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>
```

speakable_v2.hook: Maven's default lifecycle has phases that run in sequence, and each subsequent phase includes all previous ones.

speakable_v2.cap: Making these failures instead of warnings prevents hard-to-diagnose runtime problems.

questions.title: Maven Multi-Module Projects
questions.question: How do you structure a Maven multi-module project for a Java microservices monorepo?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Multi-module: parent POM aggregates multiple child modules — single build command builds all
- Parent POM: packaging=pom, lists modules, manages shared dependencies and plugins
- Module: child pom.xml inheriting from parent — no version conflicts
- Use cases: shared common module, API module, service module, integration test module
- Build selectively: -pl (projects list) + -am (also make dependencies)
- Internal dependencies: reference sibling modules by GAV coordinates
- BOM module: separate bill-of-materials to share dependency management without inheritance

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Multi-module Maven projects let you manage multiple related modules in a single repository with a single build. The parent POM defines the modules, manages shared dependency versions, and configures shared plugin settings. Each module has its own pom.xml that inherits from the parent but doesn't need to specify versions for managed dependencies.

The typical structure for a Spring Boot backend is a parent POM, a common module with shared entities and utilities, and one or more service modules that depend on common. All modules are built with one command from the root: mvn clean package. The reactor determines the correct build order based on module dependencies.

For large repositories with many modules, you can build selectively with the -pl and -am flags. If you've only changed the payment service, you run mvn -pl payment-service -am package — which builds the payment service plus any modules it depends on, skipping unrelated modules. This dramatically speeds up CI for large monorepos.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Multi-Module Structure

```
my-backend/                        ← root (parent POM)
├── pom.xml                        ← parent POM (packaging=pom)
├── common/
│   ├── pom.xml                    ← shared entities, utils, DTOs
│   └── src/
├── order-service/
│   ├── pom.xml                    ← Spring Boot app
│   └── src/
├── payment-service/
│   ├── pom.xml                    ← Spring Boot app
│   └── src/
└── integration-tests/
    └── pom.xml                    ← cross-service integration tests
```

## Parent POM

```xml
<!-- root/pom.xml -->
<project>
    <groupId>com.mycompany</groupId>
    <artifactId>my-backend</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <packaging>pom</packaging>  <!-- aggregator -->

    <modules>
        <module>common</module>
        <module>order-service</module>
        <module>payment-service</module>
        <module>integration-tests</module>
    </modules>

    <!-- Centralized dependency management for all modules -->
    <dependencyManagement>
        <dependencies>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
                <version>3.2.5</version>
                <type>pom</type>
                <scope>import</scope>
            </dependency>
        </dependencies>
    </dependencyManagement>
</project>
```

## Child Module POM

```xml
<!-- order-service/pom.xml -->
<project>
    <parent>
        <groupId>com.mycompany</groupId>
        <artifactId>my-backend</artifactId>
        <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    </parent>

    <artifactId>order-service</artifactId>
    <!-- No version needed — inherited from parent -->

    <dependencies>
        <!-- Sibling module dependency -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.mycompany</groupId>
            <artifactId>common</artifactId>
            <version>${project.version}</version>
        </dependency>
        <!-- External dependencies — versions from parent BOM -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</project>
```

## Selective Build in CI

```bash
# Build only changed service and its dependencies
mvn -pl order-service -am clean package
# -pl = projects list (comma-separated modules to build)
# -am = also make (build dependency modules first)

# Skip specific module
mvn clean package -pl '!integration-tests'

# Build all but skip tests for speed (dev only)
mvn clean package -DskipTests
```

speakable_v2.hook: Multi-module Maven projects let you manage multiple related modules in a single repository with a single build.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This dramatically speeds up CI for large monorepos.

questions.title: Maven Dependency Management and BOM
questions.question: How do you manage transitive dependency conflicts and use BOMs in Maven?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Transitive dependencies: A depends on B which depends on C — Maven includes C automatically
- Dependency mediation: nearest-wins for conflicting versions (closest to root in dep tree)
- BOM (Bill of Materials): POM with only dependencyManagement — import to align versions
- <scope>import</scope>: pull in BOM's managed versions without full parent inheritance
- exclusion: explicitly exclude transitive dependency when it causes conflict
- mvn dependency:tree: visualize full dependency tree
- mvn dependency:analyze: find unused declared and used undeclared dependencies
- maven-enforcer-plugin: fail build on dependency convergence issues

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Transitive dependency conflicts are one of the most common Maven headaches. Library A needs Jackson 2.14 and library B needs Jackson 2.12. Maven uses the nearest-wins rule — whichever version is declared closest to the root in the dependency tree wins. This can result in an older version winning even if a newer version is what your code actually needs.

BOMs solve the version alignment problem. A Bill of Materials POM declares managed versions for a family of related artifacts. When you import a BOM, those versions are used for any matching dependency in your POM without specifying a version. Spring Boot's BOM ensures all Spring components, Jackson, Hibernate, and hundreds of other libraries use tested compatible versions together.

When you have a genuine conflict that the BOM doesn't resolve, use an exclusion to block the unwanted transitive dependency and add the correct version explicitly. The maven-enforcer-plugin with dependencyConvergence fails the build if any transitive dependency appears with multiple versions in the tree — forcing you to resolve conflicts proactively.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## BOM Import

```xml
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <!-- Spring Boot BOM -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>3.2.5</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
        <!-- Testcontainers BOM -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
            <artifactId>testcontainers-bom</artifactId>
            <version>1.19.7</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <!-- Versions resolved from BOMs — no version needed -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
        <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

## Resolving Dependency Conflicts

```bash
# Visualize the dependency tree
mvn dependency:tree
mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core
# Shows which library pulls in each version of Jackson

# Find duplicates
mvn dependency:tree | grep jackson
```

```xml
<!-- Exclude conflicting transitive + override to correct version -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.some-library</groupId>
    <artifactId>some-library</artifactId>
    <version>2.5.0</version>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>

<!-- Force correct version -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
    <version>2.16.1</version>  <!-- override to the version we need -->
</dependency>
```

speakable_v2.hook: Transitive dependency conflicts are one of the most common Maven headaches.

speakable_v2.cap: The maven-enforcer-plugin with dependencyConvergence fails the build if any transitive dependency appears with multiple versions in the tree — forcing you to resolve conflicts proactively.

questions.title: Maven Profiles and Environment-Specific Builds
questions.question: How do you use Maven profiles for different build environments and configurations?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Profile: named set of build configuration activated under certain conditions
- Activation: -P flag, OS, JDK version, environment variable, property, file presence
- Common uses: different dependencies for dev vs prod, skip tests in local, CI-specific plugins
- activeByDefault: use carefully — can interfere with profile activation logic
- settings.xml profiles: credentials and mirrors — not committed to repo
- Spring profiles ≠ Maven profiles: independent, though Maven can set spring.profiles.active
- Profile inheritance: don't nest profiles; use settings.xml for secrets

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Maven profiles are named configuration blocks that can activate additional dependencies, properties, or plugin configurations depending on the build context. The most common use is environment-specific builds — a dev profile might skip slow integration tests and include development tools, while a production profile enforces all quality checks.

Profiles are activated with the -P flag on the command line, automatically based on the OS or JDK version, or when a specific file exists. The settings.xml file in the Maven user home is where team members store credentials and repository mirrors that shouldn't be committed — profiles in settings.xml can inject those credentials without exposing them in pom.xml.

It's important to distinguish Maven profiles from Spring profiles — they're completely independent. Maven profiles control the build process, while Spring profiles control the application configuration at runtime. You can use a Maven profile to set the SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE environment variable or a system property during testing, which indirectly activates Spring profiles for integration tests.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Profile Configuration

```xml
<profiles>
    <!-- Development: skip slow tests, include dev tools -->
    <profile>
        <id>dev</id>
        <activation>
            <activeByDefault>true</activeByDefault>  <!-- activated unless another profile is active -->
        </activation>
        <properties>
            <skipIntegrationTests>true</skipIntegrationTests>
        </properties>
        <dependencies>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
                <scope>runtime</scope>
                <optional>true</optional>
            </dependency>
        </dependencies>
    </profile>

    <!-- CI: run all tests, enforce quality -->
    <profile>
        <id>ci</id>
        <properties>
            <skipIntegrationTests>false</skipIntegrationTests>
        </properties>
        <build>
            <plugins>
                <plugin>
                    <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
                    <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                    <executions>
                        <execution>
                            <goals><goal>check</goal></goals>
                        </execution>
                    </executions>
                </plugin>
            </plugins>
        </build>
    </profile>

    <!-- Activated automatically on Linux (CI servers) -->
    <profile>
        <id>linux</id>
        <activation>
            <os><name>Linux</name></os>
        </activation>
        <properties>
            <integration.db.host>localhost</integration.db.host>
        </properties>
    </profile>
</profiles>
```

```bash
# Activate profile
mvn test -P ci

# Multiple profiles
mvn package -P ci,docker

# Deactivate a profile (! prefix)
mvn test -P !dev,ci
```

## settings.xml for Credentials (Not Committed)

```xml
<!-- ~/.m2/settings.xml -->
<settings>
    <servers>
        <server>
            <id>company-nexus</id>
            <username>my-username</username>
            <password>my-password</password>
        </server>
    </servers>
    <mirrors>
        <mirror>
            <id>company-nexus</id>
            <url>https://nexus.company.com/repository/maven-public/</url>
            <mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf>
        </mirror>
    </mirrors>
</settings>
```

questions.title: Maven Versioning and Release Process
questions.question: How does Maven versioning work and how do you manage releases and SNAPSHOT dependencies?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- SNAPSHOT: development version — 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT; Maven re-downloads on each build if newer
- Release: immutable — 1.0.0; once published, Maven never re-downloads
- Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH — 1.0.0, 1.1.0, 1.1.1
- maven-release-plugin: automates release process — update version, tag, deploy, bump to next SNAPSHOT
- git-commit-id-plugin: embed git SHA in artifact manifest and /actuator/info
- versions:set: update version across all modules
- SNAPSHOT dependency: avoid in production — non-deterministic builds
- Repository: SNAPSHOT repo separate from release repo in Nexus/Artifactory

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Maven SNAPSHOT versions are development builds that change frequently. When you depend on a SNAPSHOT, Maven checks the remote repository for a newer copy on every build — you always get the latest development version. This is useful during active development of shared libraries but dangerous in production builds where you need reproducibility.

Release versions are immutable. Once 1.2.0 is published to a release repository, its contents never change. This is the foundation of reproducible builds — the same version always produces the same artifact. For production deployments, always depend on release versions.

For Spring Boot microservices that you deploy as standalone applications rather than libraries, the version string in pom.xml is less critical — you identify builds by the git commit SHA embedded in the Docker image tag. But for shared libraries that other teams depend on, proper semantic versioning and a clean release process via maven-release-plugin is essential.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## SNAPSHOT vs Release

```xml
<!-- Development: 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT -->
<version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
<!-- Maven downloads latest from snapshot repo; build not reproducible -->

<!-- Release: 1.0.0 -->
<version>1.0.0</version>
<!-- Immutable; reproducible; use in production -->
```

## Maven Release Plugin

```bash
# Release process (automated by maven-release-plugin)
# 1. Check for SNAPSHOT dependencies (fail if any)
# 2. Set version to 1.0.0 (remove -SNAPSHOT)
# 3. Commit + Git tag v1.0.0
# 4. Deploy to release repository
# 5. Set version to 1.1.0-SNAPSHOT
# 6. Commit

mvn release:prepare  # steps 1-3
mvn release:perform  # steps 4-5
mvn release:clean    # clean up backup files
```

## Git Commit ID in Artifact

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>io.github.git-commit-id</groupId>
    <artifactId>git-commit-id-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals><goal>revision</goal></goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
    <configuration>
        <generateGitPropertiesFile>true</generateGitPropertiesFile>
        <generateGitPropertiesFilename>src/main/resources/git.properties</generateGitPropertiesFilename>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
```

```bash
# Exposed at /actuator/info:
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/info
# {
#   "git": {
#     "commit": {"id": "abc1234", "time": "2024-01-15T10:00:00Z"},
#     "branch": "main"
#   }
# }
```

questions.question: What are Maven lifecycle phases (validate, compile, test, package, install, deploy)?
questions.title: Maven Lifecycle Phases Explained
questions.direct_answer: Maven's default lifecycle has 23 phases executed in a fixed order. The key phases are validate (check project is correct), compile (compile source code), test (run unit tests), package (create JAR/WAR), verify (run integration tests), install (copy to local repository), and deploy (push to remote repository).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Maven's opinionated build model and can predict what happens when you run a specific phase.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking `mvn test` only runs tests — it also runs validate, initialize, generate-sources, process-sources, generate-resources, process-resources, and compile before reaching the test phase.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the three built-in lifecycles (default, clean, site), that plugin goals bind to specific phases, and that `mvn install -DskipTests` skips test execution but not compilation of test sources.

sections.title: Why Running mvn test Compiles Your Entire Project First
sections.content:
Most developers run `mvn test` expecting Maven to run their unit tests. What they don't realize is that Maven first runs validate, then processes sources, compiles all production code, processes test sources, and compiles test code — all before executing a single test. This cascading behavior is Maven's core design principle, and misunderstanding it causes confusion every time a `mvn test` build fails with a compile error.

**Maven organizes its build around three independent lifecycles.** The `default` lifecycle handles compilation through deployment across 23 fixed phases. The `clean` lifecycle removes the `target/` directory. The `site` lifecycle generates project documentation. These lifecycles are completely independent — running `mvn package` does NOT automatically clean, which is why `mvn clean package` exists as a combined command.

The key insight is that phases themselves do nothing. They are empty hooks in a fixed sequence. **Plugin goals** bind to these phases, and when Maven reaches a phase, it executes all goals bound to it.

The `maven-compiler-plugin:compile` goal binds to the `compile` phase. The `maven-surefire-plugin:test` goal binds to the `test` phase. Your POM's `<packaging>` type determines which default bindings apply — a `jar` project gets different bindings than a `war` project.

sections.title: The Cascading Chain: Every Phase Triggers Its Predecessors
sections.content:
When you run `mvn package`, Maven does not jump directly to the package phase. It executes every phase in the default lifecycle up to and including package: `validate → compile → test → package`. This means `mvn package` also compiles your code and runs your unit tests. Running `mvn deploy` executes the entire chain from validate through deploy.

The full default lifecycle has 23 phases, though most developers interact with only seven of them. The phases that matter most are `validate`, `compile`, `test`, `package`, `verify`, `install`, and `deploy` — with intermediate phases between them for source generation, resource processing, and test compilation.

**The three lifecycles never cascade into each other.** Running `mvn install` executes the default lifecycle through install, but it does NOT clean the `target/` directory first. This is why stale class files from deleted source files can cause mysterious test failures — the old `.class` files remain in `target/` from a previous build. The fix is the ubiquitous `mvn clean install`, which runs the clean lifecycle first, then the default lifecycle through install.

Understanding the cascade also explains the `-DskipTests` vs `-Dmaven.test.skip=true` difference. The flag `-DskipTests` tells Surefire to skip test execution but still compiles test classes — catching compile errors early. The flag `-Dmaven.test.skip=true` skips both compilation and execution, which is faster but can hide broken test code.

sections.title: Plugin Goals Are the Workers — Phases Are Just Hooks
sections.content:
Phases define when work happens. Plugin goals define what work happens. The `compile` phase has no built-in behavior — it is a slot where `maven-compiler-plugin:compile` is bound by default when your project uses `<packaging>jar</packaging>`.

You can bind custom goals to any phase. This is how code generation, coverage instrumentation, and static analysis integrate into the build. **JaCoCo's** `prepare-agent` goal binds to the `initialize` phase to instrument bytecode before compilation, and its `report` goal binds to `verify` to generate coverage reports after integration tests complete.

The binding configuration lives in your POM's `<build><plugins>` section, where each `<execution>` block maps a goal to a phase.

```xml
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
  <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <phase>initialize</phase>
      <goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals>
    </execution>
    <execution>
      <phase>verify</phase>
      <goals><goal>report</goal></goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
```

**Multiple goals can bind to the same phase** and execute in POM declaration order. This ordering matters — if a code generator binds to `generate-sources` and Lombok's annotation processor also runs during compilation, the generator must be declared first to ensure generated files exist before the compiler processes annotations.

sections.title: The Test vs Verify Split That Most Teams Get Wrong
sections.content:
Maven has two test phases served by two different plugins, and confusing them is one of the most common build configuration mistakes. The `test` phase runs **`maven-surefire-plugin`**, which executes classes matching `*Test.java`. The `verify` phase runs **`maven-failsafe-plugin`**, which executes classes matching `*IT.java`.

The split exists for a practical reason. Integration tests often need external resources — databases, message brokers, application servers — that must be started before the tests and shut down afterward. The lifecycle provides `pre-integration-test` for startup, `integration-test` for execution, and `post-integration-test` for cleanup. **Failsafe deliberately delays reporting failures** until the `verify` phase, ensuring cleanup runs even when tests fail.

The practical consequence for Spring Boot teams: `@SpringBootTest` classes should be named `*IT.java` and executed by Failsafe during `mvn verify`, not by Surefire during `mvn test`. Spring context startup takes seconds per test class, and mixing slow integration tests with fast unit tests defeats the purpose of `mvn test` as a quick feedback loop.

For CI pipelines, the distinction drives which command to run. Developers use `mvn test` for fast local feedback. The CI pipeline runs `mvn verify` to include integration tests. The full deploy stage runs `mvn deploy`, which cascades through everything. Using `mvn install -pl :service -am` targets a single module and its dependencies, keeping the inner development loop fast.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cascading execution: `mvn package` = validate + compile + test + package** — running any phase triggers all preceding phases in that lifecycle, which is why `mvn test` also compiles your code and why compile errors surface during test runs
- **Three independent lifecycles (default, clean, site)** — they never cascade into each other; `mvn package` does NOT clean the `target/` directory, hence the universal habit of `mvn clean package`
- **Phases are hooks, plugin goals do the work** — `maven-compiler-plugin:compile` binds to the compile phase; your `<packaging>` type determines which default bindings Maven applies automatically
- **Surefire (`test` phase) vs Failsafe (`verify` phase)** — Surefire runs `*Test.java` for unit tests; Failsafe runs `*IT.java` for integration tests with guaranteed cleanup between `integration-test` and `verify`
- **`-DskipTests` still compiles test code** — it skips execution but catches compile errors, unlike `-Dmaven.test.skip=true` which skips both; prefer `-DskipTests` in CI for safety

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Maven's lifecycle is the mental model that explains why running `mvn test` also compiles your code, and why running `mvn package` runs your tests. Phases are not independent commands — they cascade.

**The cascade rule**
- Running any phase executes every preceding phase in the lifecycle first — `mvn test` triggers validate, compile, process-test-resources, test-compile, and then test; a compile error surfaces when you run `mvn test` because compile runs first
- The three lifecycles are independent and do not cascade into each other: `default` (build and deploy), `clean` (remove target/), and `site` (documentation); `mvn clean package` is two separate lifecycle invocations, not one
- This is why `mvn clean package` is the CI standard and not just `mvn package` — without `clean`, leftover compiled classes from a renamed or deleted source file can silently stay in the build

**Phases are empty hooks bound by plugins**
- A phase by itself does nothing; it is a slot that plugin goals bind to — `maven-compiler-plugin:compile` binds to `compile`, `maven-surefire-plugin:test` binds to `test`
- You bind custom goals to phases in the POM: adding JaCoCo to the `test` phase generates coverage data automatically without a separate Maven invocation
- `mvn help:describe -Dcmd=test` lists every goal bound to a given phase, which is how you diagnose why a phase is slower than expected

**The most useful phase distinctions**
- `package` creates the JAR without installing to `~/.m2`; `install` adds it to the local repository so other local projects can depend on it; `deploy` uploads to a remote repository for other teams
- `verify` runs integration tests and quality checks after `package` — use `mvn clean verify` in CI, not `mvn clean package`, so integration tests and coverage gates are part of every build

questions.title: Maven Dependency Scopes: compile, test, provided, runtime
questions.direct_answer: Maven dependency scopes control which classpath a dependency appears on and whether it is included in the packaged artifact. `compile` (default) is everywhere; `test` is test classpath only; `provided` is compile classpath but excluded from the package (container provides it); `runtime` is runtime and package but not compile.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `compile` scope for a Servlet API or Lombok dependency that should be `provided`, which causes conflicts when the artifact is deployed to an application server.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the `import` scope for importing BOMs (Bill of Materials) in `<dependencyManagement>`, and the `system` scope (deprecated, avoid), and how transitive scope rules work (e.g. a `runtime` dependency of a `compile` dependency becomes `runtime` in your project).

sections.title: Four Classpaths, One Wrong Scope, and a ClassNotFoundException in Production
sections.content:
A dependency that works perfectly during development can cause a `ClassNotFoundException` the moment it reaches production. The root cause is almost always a scope mismatch — a JAR that was available on the compile classpath during development is missing from the runtime classpath in the deployed artifact. Maven dependency scopes exist to prevent exactly this problem by controlling which classpath each dependency appears on and whether it ships in the final package.

**The four scopes you need for most projects are `compile`, `test`, `provided`, and `runtime`.** Each scope answers three questions: is this dependency available during compilation, is it available at runtime, and does it end up in the packaged JAR or WAR? Getting these answers wrong has concrete consequences. Declaring the Servlet API as `compile` instead of `provided` means your WAR ships a Servlet API JAR that conflicts with the one Tomcat provides, causing mysterious class-loading errors.

Declaring a JDBC driver as `compile` instead of `runtime` works fine but leaks the driver's internal classes onto your compile classpath, letting developers accidentally import implementation classes instead of coding against `java.sql` interfaces.

Two additional scopes serve specialized purposes. The **`import`** scope, valid only inside `<dependencyManagement>` with `<type>pom</type>`, imports version recommendations from a BOM like `spring-boot-dependencies` without adding any actual dependency. The `system` scope is deprecated and should be avoided — it references a JAR by absolute path, making builds non-portable.

sections.title: Which Classpath Each Scope Controls — The Decision Matrix
sections.content:
Understanding exactly which classpath each scope affects is the key to avoiding runtime surprises. The table below maps each scope to its visibility during compilation, testing, runtime, and packaging.

| Scope | Compile CP | Test CP | Runtime CP | In Package | Transitive |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **compile** (default) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| **test** | No | Yes | No | No | No |
| **provided** | Yes | Yes | No | No | No |
| **runtime** | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes (runtime only) |
| **import** | N/A | N/A | N/A | N/A | `<dependencyManagement>` only |

The most commonly confused pair is **`provided` vs `runtime`** because they are near-opposites. Provided means the dependency is needed to compile your code but excluded from the package because the deployment environment supplies it — the Servlet API on Tomcat, or Lombok which only runs during annotation processing. Runtime means the dependency is not needed to compile but must be present when the application runs — JDBC drivers are the textbook case because you code against `java.sql.DataSource` interfaces, never importing the driver class directly.

**Transitive scope mediation** adds another layer. When your project depends on library A at `compile` scope, and library A depends on library B at `runtime` scope, Maven applies mediation rules: B becomes `runtime` in your project. A `test`-scoped dependency of any library is never inherited. This is why `NoClassDefFoundError` sometimes appears at runtime — a transitive dependency expected by a library was scoped as `provided` in that library's POM, and your environment doesn't supply it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`compile` (default) goes on all three classpaths** — the dependency is available during compilation, testing, and runtime, and is packaged into the artifact; use it for anything your code directly imports and calls
- **`provided` compiles but does not package** — needed at compile time but excluded from the deployed artifact because the runtime environment supplies it; misusing `compile` for the Servlet API causes class-loading conflicts on Tomcat
- **`runtime` packages but does not compile** — the opposite of provided; JDBC drivers should always be `runtime` scope to prevent developers from importing driver-internal classes instead of coding against `java.sql` interfaces
- **`import` scope pulls in a BOM without adding a dependency** — valid only in `<dependencyManagement>` with `<type>pom</type>`; this is how `spring-boot-dependencies` manages hundreds of library versions centrally
- **Transitive scope mediation can silently remove classes** — a `runtime` dependency of your `compile` dependency becomes `runtime` in your project; a `provided` dependency is never inherited, causing `NoClassDefFoundError` if your environment doesn't supply it

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Maven's five dependency scopes control which classpaths a dependency appears on and whether it ships in the packaged artifact. Getting scopes wrong is a common source of both bloated artifacts and production `ClassNotFoundException` errors.

**Compile and test — the most common scopes**
- `compile` (the default) goes on every classpath: compile, test, and runtime; it ships in the final JAR — use it for core libraries your code directly imports and consumers of your library also need
- `test` restricts the dependency to test compilation and execution only — JUnit, Mockito, AssertJ belong here; they never appear in the final package and never reach production; forgetting `test` scope on Mockito ships it to production unnecessarily
- `runtime` is not needed to compile but must be on the runtime classpath — JDBC drivers fit perfectly because you code against `java.sql` interfaces, not the driver classes; compile scope on a driver adds unnecessary compile-time coupling

**Provided — the shared-runtime trap**
- `provided` means the container or runtime environment supplies the dependency — the Servlet API on Tomcat, Lombok during annotation processing; the dependency is on the compile classpath but excluded from the final package
- Packaging a Spring Boot fat JAR with Tomcat as `compile` scope includes an embedded container; packaging it as `provided` correctly excludes it when deploying to an external Tomcat
- Lombok must be `provided` (or `optional`) — including it as `compile` ships it to consumers of your library who may be using a different version

**Scope verification before deployment**
- `mvn dependency:tree -Dscope=runtime` shows exactly what ships in the final artifact — run this before every release to catch accidentally included test or compile-only dependencies
- The most painful scope bugs surface as `ClassNotFoundException` in production: a library was `provided` in a context where no container supplied it, or `test` scoped in a module that shipped it to a WAR

questions.question: How does Maven POM inheritance and aggregation work?
questions.title: Maven POM Inheritance and Aggregation
questions.direct_answer: POM inheritance allows a child module to inherit configuration (dependencies, plugins, properties) from a parent POM declared with `<parent>`. POM aggregation allows a root POM declared with `<modules>` to build multiple child modules together. A POM can be both a parent and an aggregator, but they serve distinct purposes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand how to share configuration across modules without duplication and how multi-module builds are orchestrated.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing inheritance (configuration sharing) with aggregation (build orchestration). A child can inherit from a parent that is not in the same build, and an aggregator can include modules that have a different parent.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Spring Boot's `spring-boot-starter-parent` uses POM inheritance to provide dependency management, plugin configuration defaults, and resource filtering. Also mention `<relativePath>` in the `<parent>` block.

sections.title: The Difference Between Sharing Configuration and Orchestrating Builds
sections.content:
Imagine a Java project with ten microservices, all using Spring Boot 3.2, Java 17, and the same Checkstyle configuration. Without POM inheritance, changing the Spring Boot version means editing ten `pom.xml` files — and inevitably someone forgets one, creating a version drift that surfaces as a `MethodNotFoundException` in production.

**POM inheritance** solves configuration sharing. A child POM declares a `<parent>` block and automatically inherits `<properties>`, `<dependencyManagement>`, `<pluginManagement>`, and default plugin configurations. Change the Spring Boot version once in the parent, and all children pick it up.

**POM aggregation** solves a different problem: build orchestration. An aggregator POM lists submodules in a `<modules>` block. Running `mvn install` at the root discovers all modules, resolves the dependency order between them, and builds them in the correct sequence. Without aggregation, you would manually build each module in dependency order.

The critical point most candidates miss: **these are orthogonal relationships**. A child can inherit from a parent in a completely different repository — `spring-boot-starter-parent` is the classic example. An aggregator can list modules that have different parents. The most common pattern combines both roles in a single root POM, but understanding they are independent concepts is what the interviewer is testing.

sections.title: Inheritance vs Aggregation: Two Problems, Two Mechanisms
sections.content:
Each mechanism has a distinct purpose, and confusing them leads to build configurations that are either fragile or excessively verbose.

| Dimension | Inheritance (`<parent>`) | Aggregation (`<modules>`) |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Share configuration across POMs | Build multiple modules together |
| Declared by | Child POM via `<parent>` block | Root POM via `<modules>` block |
| Direction | Child points up to parent | Parent points down to children |
| Configuration shared | Properties, dependency versions, plugin defaults | Nothing — only build inclusion |
| Required POM packaging | Parent must be `<packaging>pom</packaging>` | Aggregator must be `<packaging>pom</packaging>` |
| Cross-repo support | Yes — inherit from any published POM | Modules must be on the local filesystem |
| Classic example | `spring-boot-starter-parent` | Your project's root `pom.xml` |

The **`<dependencyManagement>`** block in a parent POM defines versions without adding dependencies. Children still must declare the dependency in their `<dependencies>` section but can omit the `<version>` tag — the parent's managed version applies. This is distinct from declaring a dependency directly in the parent's `<dependencies>`, which would force every child to inherit that dependency whether they need it or not.

**`<pluginManagement>`** works the same way for plugins: the parent sets version and configuration defaults, but children must still reference the plugin in their `<build><plugins>` section to activate it. This two-step pattern — declare defaults in management, activate in the child — is Maven's way of balancing consistency with flexibility.

sections.title: When to Combine Both Roles vs Keep Them Separate
sections.content:
The typical Java project uses a **single root POM as both parent and aggregator**. It lists child modules in `<modules>` and provides `<dependencyManagement>` and `<pluginManagement>` for configuration inheritance. This works well for monorepo layouts where all modules share the same Spring Boot version, Java version, and build conventions.

Separating the roles becomes valuable in two scenarios. First, when your modules should inherit from an external parent like `spring-boot-starter-parent` for its dependency management and sensible defaults. In this case, your root POM is the aggregator only, and children point their `<parent>` to the Spring Boot parent.

Second, when building a **BOM-only parent** for a library ecosystem. A parent POM published to Nexus provides version management for all libraries in your organization. Consumer projects inherit from it for consistent versions, but they are not aggregated — they live in separate repositories with independent build cycles.

The `<relativePath>` element in the child's `<parent>` block controls where Maven looks for the parent POM. Without it, Maven searches the local `~/.m2/repository` first, which fails on fresh checkouts. Setting `<relativePath>../pom.xml</relativePath>` tells Maven to look on the filesystem, which is essential during development.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Inheritance (`<parent>`) shares configuration** — properties, managed dependency versions, and plugin defaults flow from parent to child, eliminating copy-paste drift across modules when upgrading Spring Boot or Java versions
- **Aggregation (`<modules>`) orchestrates builds** — the root POM lists submodules and the Maven Reactor resolves build order automatically; modules must exist on the local filesystem
- **`<dependencyManagement>` defines versions without adding dependencies** — children still must declare the dependency in `<dependencies>` but omit the version; this is different from declaring a dependency directly in the parent, which forces all children to inherit it
- **Inheritance and aggregation are independent** — a child can inherit from a parent in a different repository (like `spring-boot-starter-parent`), and an aggregator can include modules with different parents
- **`<relativePath>` prevents fresh-checkout failures** — without it, Maven looks for the parent POM in `~/.m2/repository` first, which fails on clean clones; set it to the filesystem path of the parent POM

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
POM inheritance and aggregation look like the same thing from a distance but solve completely different problems. Inheritance is about sharing configuration — a parent POM defines managed dependency versions and plugin defaults that children inherit. Aggregation is about build orchestration — a root POM lists submodules and Maven builds them in the correct order.

**Inheritance — configuration sharing**
- When a child POM declares `<parent>`, it inherits properties, plugin configuration, and `<dependencyManagement>` from the parent — inheriting from `spring-boot-starter-parent` gives you aligned versions for all Spring and Jackson libraries without declaring a single version yourself
- `<dependencyManagement>` defines which version to use without pulling the dependency in — children still explicitly declare what they need; the parent only controls which version is selected when they do
- A child can inherit from a parent in a completely different repository — that is exactly what every Spring Boot project does with `spring-boot-starter-parent`; the parent does not need to be part of the same build

**Aggregation — build orchestration**
- The root POM's `<modules>` block lists subproject directories; running `mvn install` at the root triggers the Maven Reactor, which computes dependency order automatically
- If `service` depends on `core`, Reactor builds `core` first without any explicit ordering configuration — it infers order from `<dependency>` references between modules
- The most useful Reactor command is `mvn install -pl :service -am` — it builds only the target module and its dependencies, skipping unrelated modules; essential in large multi-module projects with slow full builds

**Combining both roles**
- Most projects combine both in the root POM: `<packaging>pom</packaging>` with both a `<modules>` block and a `<dependencyManagement>` section
- The two mechanisms are independent — you can aggregate modules that inherit from different parents, and you can inherit from a parent without being part of its aggregation

questions.question: How do you manage transitive dependencies and conflict resolution?
questions.title: Maven Transitive Dependencies and Conflict Resolution
questions.direct_answer: Maven resolves version conflicts using nearest-definition wins: the version of a transitive dependency declared at the shallowest depth in the dependency tree wins. You resolve conflicts explicitly by declaring the desired version directly in your `<dependencies>` (nearest win) or enforcing it via `<dependencyManagement>` (centralized version management).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can diagnose dependency conflicts — a frequent source of runtime errors — and know the tools to fix them.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `<exclusions>` to remove a transitive dependency without declaring the desired version, which can result in a missing class at runtime instead of resolving the conflict.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention `mvn dependency:tree`, `mvn dependency:analyze` (detects declared-but-unused and used-but-undeclared dependencies), and the Maven Enforcer plugin's `requireUpperBoundDeps` rule to catch version downgrades.

sections.title: The Runtime Error That Compiles Fine: Why Version Conflicts Are Maven’s Worst Trap
sections.content:
Your Spring Boot application compiles without warnings, passes all unit tests, and then throws `NoSuchMethodError` in production. The stack trace points to a method in `jackson-databind` that clearly exists — you can see it in the source code. But Maven silently selected version 2.12 instead of 2.14, and that method was only added in 2.13.

**Transitive dependency conflicts** are Maven's most dangerous failure mode because they are invisible at compile time. Maven resolves version conflicts using the **nearest-definition-wins** rule: the version declared at the shallowest depth in the dependency tree takes precedence. If your POM declares library A which depends on `jackson-databind:2.14`, and library B which depends on `jackson-databind:2.12`, both references exist at depth 2. When two dependencies sit at the same depth, Maven picks the one declared first in the POM.

The result is deterministic but not intuitive. Simply reordering `<dependency>` entries in your POM can change which version Maven selects, and the wrong version might be missing methods, classes, or behaviors that your code or another library expects. The compiler cannot catch this because it compiles against whichever version Maven resolved — the mismatch only reveals itself when the JVM tries to load a class or invoke a method that doesn't exist in the selected version.

sections.title: Diagnosing the Conflict: mvn dependency:tree Is Your X-Ray
sections.content:
The first step when you suspect a version conflict is running `mvn dependency:tree` with a filter to isolate the suspect library. This shows every path that pulls in the dependency and which version Maven selected.

For a Jackson conflict, the diagnostic command reveals exactly which libraries pull in conflicting versions.

```bash
mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind
```

The output shows something like `jackson-databind:2.12.0` selected via `library-b` at depth 2, with `jackson-databind:2.14.0` omitted from the `library-a` path. Adding the `-Dverbose` flag shows the rejected alternatives explicitly, making the conflict visible.

**`mvn dependency:analyze`** catches a different class of problem. It reports two categories: **used-but-undeclared** dependencies (your code imports classes from a transitive dependency that could disappear if a library drops it) and **declared-but-unused** dependencies (you declared it explicitly but no code references it). The used-but-undeclared category is particularly dangerous — your code depends on a transitive dependency that your direct dependency could remove at any time, breaking your build with no change on your end.

The Maven Enforcer plugin adds proactive prevention. Its `requireUpperBoundDeps` rule fails the build whenever any transitive dependency resolves to a version lower than the highest version requested in the graph. This catches silent downgrades before they cause runtime errors.

sections.title: Three Fixes, Ranked by Cleanliness
sections.content:
Once you identify the conflict, three resolution strategies exist with different trade-offs.

The cleanest approach is **`<dependencyManagement>`**. Declaring a version in the parent POM's `<dependencyManagement>` section overrides all transitive references across the entire dependency graph. Every module in the project resolves that artifact to the managed version, regardless of what individual libraries request. This is the approach Spring Boot uses — its parent POM manages hundreds of dependency versions so all Spring modules remain compatible.

```xml
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
      <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
      <version>2.16.1</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
```

This pins `jackson-databind` to 2.16.1 everywhere in the project, regardless of what any transitive dependency requests.

The second approach is **direct declaration**. Adding the dependency explicitly in your `<dependencies>` section at depth 1 wins by the nearest-definition rule over any transitive reference at depth 2 or deeper. This is quick but local — it only fixes the conflict in one module, not across a multi-module project.

The third approach is **`<exclusions>`** on a specific dependency path. You exclude the unwanted transitive version from a particular library and re-add the desired version as a direct dependency. This is surgical but brittle — if you exclude without re-adding, you get `ClassNotFoundException` instead of a version conflict.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Nearest-definition-wins resolves version conflicts** — Maven picks the version declared at the shallowest depth in the dependency tree; at equal depth, the first-declared dependency in the POM wins, making declaration order silently significant
- **`mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=groupId:artifactId` is the diagnostic tool** — filters the full tree to show every path pulling in a specific artifact and which version Maven selected; add `-Dverbose` to see rejected alternatives
- **`<dependencyManagement>` is the cleanest fix** — pins a version centrally so every module and every transitive path resolves to it, which is exactly how Spring Boot's parent POM manages hundreds of compatible library versions
- **`<exclusions>` without re-adding causes `ClassNotFoundException`** — excluding a transitive dependency removes it from the classpath entirely; always declare the desired version as a direct dependency after excluding the conflicting one
- **Maven Enforcer's `requireUpperBoundDeps` catches silent downgrades** — fails the build when any transitive dependency resolves to a version lower than the highest requested, preventing the exact class of bug that causes `NoSuchMethodError` in production

sections.content:

**How Maven resolves conflicts**
- Maven's nearest-definition-wins rule: the version declared at the shallowest depth in the dependency tree wins — a direct `<dependency>` at depth 1 beats a transitive dependency at depth 3 regardless of version numbers
- When two versions appear at the same depth, the first-declared dependency in the POM wins — simply reordering `<dependency>` blocks can change which library version you compile against, which is why the behavior feels non-deterministic
- `mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind` filters the tree to one library, immediately showing which paths pull in which versions and which one Maven selected

**The canonical fixes**
- `<dependencyManagement>` in the root POM overrides all transitive references — declaring a version there is the authoritative fix that applies across the entire module graph; this is how Spring Boot's parent POM pins hundreds of library versions
- Declaring the dependency directly at depth 1 wins by the nearest-definition rule — a quick fix for a single module, but `<dependencyManagement>` is preferable in multi-module projects
- `<exclusions>` removes a transitive dependency entirely — use only when you need the library absent, not just at a different version; excluding without re-declaring a version leaves the classpath incomplete

**Preventing conflicts in CI**
- The Maven Enforcer plugin with `requireUpperBoundDeps` fails the build when a transitive dependency resolves to a version lower than the highest requested — it catches silent downgrades before they become production incidents
- Run `mvn dependency:analyze` to find declared but unused dependencies and used but undeclared transitive dependencies — both categories are maintenance risks

questions.question: How do you create a multi-module Maven project?
questions.title: Creating a Multi-Module Maven Project
questions.direct_answer: A multi-module Maven project has a root POM with `<packaging>pom</packaging>` that lists submodules in `<modules>`. Each submodule is a subdirectory with its own `pom.xml` that declares the root as its `<parent>`. Running `mvn install` at the root builds all modules in dependency order.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can structure a large Java application into cohesive, independently-buildable modules.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not specifying `<relativePath>` in the child's `<parent>` block, causing Maven to look in the local repository for the parent POM instead of the local file system during development.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention using `<dependencyManagement>` in the parent to centralize versions, building individual modules with `mvn install -pl :module-name -am` (`-am` builds dependency modules first), and the Maven Reactor for build ordering.

sections.title: Why Splitting a Monolith POM Into Modules Prevents the Everything-Rebuilds Problem
sections.content:
A Java project that starts as a single module works fine until it reaches a certain size. At 50,000 lines and 200 classes, running `mvn test` takes three minutes because it compiles and tests everything, even when you only changed one service class. The compile-test-fix loop slows to a crawl, and developers start skipping tests entirely.

**A multi-module Maven project** splits the codebase into independent modules — `core`, `persistence`, `service`, `web` — each with its own `pom.xml`, its own source tree, and its own test suite. A root POM with `<packaging>pom</packaging>` acts as both the aggregator (listing modules for build orchestration) and the parent (providing shared configuration through `<dependencyManagement>` and `<pluginManagement>`).

The **Maven Reactor** reads all POM files, resolves inter-module dependencies, and determines the correct build order. If `service` depends on `core`, the Reactor builds `core` first regardless of declaration order in `<modules>`. During development, `mvn install -pl :service -am` builds only the `service` module and its upstream dependencies, skipping `web` and `batch` modules entirely. This targeted build is what restores the fast feedback loop — you rebuild and test only what you changed.

sections.title: The Root POM: Aggregation and Inheritance in One File
sections.content:
The root POM serves double duty. Its `<modules>` block tells the Reactor which subdirectories contain child modules. Its **`<dependencyManagement>`** block centralizes dependency versions so children never hardcode them. The root must declare `<packaging>pom</packaging>` — without this, Maven treats it as a JAR project and refuses to list modules.

A typical Spring Boot multi-module root POM imports the Spring Boot BOM via `<dependencyManagement>` and sets shared properties for Java version and encoding.

```xml
<project>
  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>my-app</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
  <packaging>pom</packaging>

  <modules>
    <module>core</module>
    <module>service</module>
    <module>web</module>
  </modules>

  <properties>
    <java.version>17</java.version>
  </properties>

  <dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
      <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
        <version>3.2.0</version>
        <type>pom</type>
        <scope>import</scope>
      </dependency>
    </dependencies>
  </dependencyManagement>
</project>
```

Children inherit `groupId` and `version` from this parent, so each child POM only needs to declare its own `artifactId` and specific dependencies. The BOM import means no child module needs to specify a version for any Spring-managed dependency.

sections.title: Child POMs: Inheriting From the Parent and Referencing Siblings
sections.content:
Each child module's `pom.xml` declares the root as its `<parent>` and uses `<relativePath>` to locate it on the filesystem. Without `<relativePath>`, Maven looks for the parent in `~/.m2/repository` first, which fails on fresh clones from version control.

Inter-module dependencies use the same Maven coordinates as any other dependency, with `${project.version}` keeping versions synchronized with the parent.

```xml
<project>
  <parent>
    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>my-app</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <relativePath>../pom.xml</relativePath>
  </parent>

  <artifactId>service</artifactId>

  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>com.example</groupId>
      <artifactId>core</artifactId>
      <version>${project.version}</version>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</project>
```

The `spring-boot-starter` dependency needs no version because the parent's BOM import manages it. The `core` dependency uses `${project.version}` to automatically stay synchronized when the Maven Release Plugin bumps versions across all modules.

sections.title: Targeted Builds: The Commands That Save You Thirty Minutes a Day
sections.content:
The Reactor's `-pl` (project list) and `-am` (also make dependencies) flags are essential for productive development in multi-module projects.

Running `mvn install -pl :service -am` builds only the `service` module plus any modules it depends on (`core` in this case), skipping `web` and any other modules entirely. This is the command you use during development — it cuts a three-minute full build down to thirty seconds. The `-am` flag ensures upstream dependencies are fresh, so you never compile against stale artifacts.

When a full build fails partway through, `mvn install -rf :web` resumes from the `web` module, skipping modules that already built successfully. This avoids re-running the first five minutes of a ten-module build when only the last module has a test failure.

For **parallel builds**, `mvn install -T 1C` allocates one thread per CPU core. Modules without dependencies on each other build concurrently, cutting build times by 50-70% on projects with independent modules. Combine with `-pl :service -am` for maximum speed during development.

One production warning: **`install` copies artifacts to `~/.m2/repository`**, which is necessary for sibling module resolution. Running only `mvn compile` in a multi-module project can fail because sibling dependencies look in the local repository, not the build output directory. Always use `install` or `package` for multi-module builds.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Root POM needs `<packaging>pom</packaging>`** — without this, Maven treats it as a JAR project and refuses to aggregate child modules; the root provides both build orchestration via `<modules>` and configuration inheritance via `<dependencyManagement>`
- **`<relativePath>` prevents fresh-clone build failures** — the child's `<parent>` block must include a `<relativePath>` pointing to the parent POM on disk, otherwise Maven searches `~/.m2/repository` first and fails on clean checkouts
- **`${project.version}` keeps sibling versions synchronized** — inter-module dependencies should use this property instead of hardcoding version strings; the Maven Release Plugin updates all versions atomically when releasing
- **`mvn install -pl :service -am` is the developer's key command** — `-pl` targets a single module and `-am` (also make) builds its upstream dependencies, cutting multi-minute full builds down to seconds during development
- **Maven Reactor resolves build order automatically** — it reads all module POMs, builds a dependency graph, and executes in topological order; `service` depending on `core` means `core` builds first regardless of `<modules>` declaration order

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A multi-module Maven project uses a root POM to orchestrate the build and share configuration across related modules. The key is understanding what the root POM does and what each child declares itself.

**Root POM structure**
- The root POM uses `<packaging>pom</packaging>` and serves two separate roles: the `<modules>` block lists child directories for Reactor build orchestration, and `<dependencyManagement>` defines shared dependency versions that children inherit
- `<relativePath>` in the child's `<parent>` block points to the parent POM location on the filesystem — without it, Maven looks in `~/.m2/repository` first, which fails on fresh checkouts before the parent has been installed locally
- Inter-module dependencies use `${project.version}` to stay synchronized — hardcoding a version in a module reference means you must update it manually every release

**Maven Reactor — build ordering**
- The Reactor analyzes `<dependency>` references between modules to determine build order automatically — `service` depending on `core` means `core` always compiles first
- `mvn install -pl :service -am` builds the target module and all its upstream dependencies, skipping unrelated modules — the most useful productivity command in large multi-module projects
- `mvn install -pl :service,core -amd` builds a module and everything that depends on it downstream — useful for validating a change ripples correctly through consumers

**Shared configuration best practices**
- Define all dependency versions in `<dependencyManagement>` at the root — children declare what they need, the root controls which version; no version drift between modules
- Define plugin configuration in `<pluginManagement>` at the root and bind plugins in child POMs — this separates "what version of the plugin" from "which modules use it"
- Never commit Nexus credentials to the root POM — keep the `<distributionManagement>` URL in the POM and credentials in `~/.m2/settings.xml` or CI environment variables
