questions.question: How do you use Maven profiles for environment-specific builds?
questions.title: Maven Profiles for Environment-Specific Builds
questions.direct_answer: Maven profiles are POM sections that activate conditionally to modify build configuration. You define them with `<profiles><profile>` blocks in `pom.xml` or `settings.xml`, activate them with `-P profile-id` on the command line or via automatic activation conditions (OS, property, file presence).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand how to vary build behavior across environments without maintaining multiple POMs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting sensitive credentials directly in `pom.xml` profiles instead of in `~/.m2/settings.xml` (which is not committed to version control).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention automatic activation by property (`-Dproperty=value`), OS, or JDK version; the `<activeByDefault>` flag and its pitfall (it deactivates when any other profile is activated); and using Spring Boot profiles alongside Maven profiles.

sections.title: One POM, Multiple Environments — Without Maintaining Separate Build Files
sections.content:
Before Maven profiles, teams maintained multiple build configurations — one POM for development, one for staging, one for production. When a dependency version changed, every configuration file needed updating. The drift between environments caused bugs that only appeared in production, never locally.

**Maven profiles** solve this by letting you define conditional sections within a single POM. A profile can override properties, add dependencies, activate plugins, or change resource filtering — and it activates based on a command-line flag, a system property, an environment variable, the OS, or the JDK version. The most common use case is switching database URLs and Spring profiles between dev, CI, and production environments.

The mechanism works through property overrides. A `dev` profile sets `<spring.profiles.active>dev</spring.profiles.active>` and `<skip.integration.tests>true</skip.integration.tests>`. A `ci` profile flips those values and adds JaCoCo coverage analysis. The same POM produces different build behaviors depending on which profile activates.

**The most dangerous mistake with profiles is putting credentials in `pom.xml`**. Database passwords, Nexus tokens, and signing keys must go in `~/.m2/settings.xml`, which is local to each machine and never committed to version control. Properties defined in `settings.xml` profiles are accessible in `pom.xml` via standard `${property}` syntax, giving you the configuration flexibility without the security risk.

sections.title: Activation Mechanisms: From Explicit Flags to Automatic Environment Detection
sections.content:
Profiles activate through several mechanisms, and choosing the right one prevents configuration drift across environments.

**Command-line activation** with `-P` is the simplest: `mvn install -Prelease` activates the `release` profile. You can combine profiles with `-Pci,release` and deactivate with `-P!dev`. This approach works well for profiles that represent explicit build modes.

**Property-based activation** ties a profile to a system property or environment variable. A CI profile can activate automatically when the `CI` environment variable is present, which GitHub Actions, Jenkins, and GitLab CI all set by default.

```xml
<profile>
  <id>ci</id>
  <activation>
    <property>
      <name>env.CI</name>
    </property>
  </activation>
  <properties>
    <skip.integration.tests>false</skip.integration.tests>
  </properties>
</profile>
```

This eliminates the need for CI pipeline scripts to pass `-Pci` explicitly — the profile activates automatically in any CI environment.

**The `<activeByDefault>` trap** catches many teams. Setting `<activeByDefault>true</activeByDefault>` on a `dev` profile seems reasonable, but the flag silently deactivates the moment any other profile is explicitly activated. If a CI engineer runs `mvn install -Prelease`, the dev profile quietly turns off. Prefer environment-variable-based activation or explicit `-P` flags to avoid this subtle behavior change.

sections.title: Credentials Belong in settings.xml — The Production Footgun Everyone Hits Once
sections.content:
The most common security mistake with Maven profiles is declaring deployment credentials directly in `pom.xml`. This seems convenient — the Nexus password sits next to the Nexus URL — but `pom.xml` is committed to version control. The credentials become visible to every developer with repository access, and if the repository is public, they are exposed to the internet.

**The correct pattern separates URLs from credentials.** The `pom.xml` profile declares the Nexus repository URL and a server ID. The `~/.m2/settings.xml` file, which is local to each machine and never committed, stores the actual credentials under a matching `<server>` entry.

```xml
<!-- settings.xml (local, never committed) -->
<servers>
  <server>
    <id>nexus-releases</id>
    <username>${env.NEXUS_USER}</username>
    <password>${env.NEXUS_PASS}</password>
  </server>
</servers>
```

In CI environments, `settings.xml` is generated dynamically using pipeline secrets injected as environment variables. The `${env.NEXUS_USER}` syntax references environment variables directly, so the actual password never exists in any file on disk.

Run `mvn help:active-profiles` to verify which profiles are active in the current build context. This command is invaluable when debugging unexpected behavior — it shows exactly which profiles Maven activated and through which mechanism. When a build behaves differently in CI than locally, the active profile list is the first thing to check.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`-P` activates profiles explicitly** — `mvn install -Prelease` turns on the release profile; combine with `-Pci,release` or deactivate with `-P!dev`; this is the most predictable activation method
- **`<activeByDefault>` silently deactivates when any profile is explicit** — if your dev profile is active by default and someone runs `-Prelease`, the dev profile quietly turns off, changing build behavior in ways that are hard to debug
- **Credentials in `pom.xml` is a security incident waiting to happen** — repository passwords, signing keys, and API tokens must live in `~/.m2/settings.xml` (never committed); reference environment variables with `${env.VAR_NAME}` for CI
- **Property-based activation detects CI automatically** — a profile with `<activation><property><name>env.CI</name></property></activation>` activates in any CI system that sets the `CI` environment variable, eliminating pipeline-specific `-P` flags
- **`mvn help:active-profiles` debugs unexpected build behavior** — shows exactly which profiles Maven activated and through which mechanism; check this first when builds behave differently in CI versus locally

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Maven profiles let you activate different POM sections based on flags, environment variables, or conditions — the standard mechanism for varying build behavior between developer machines and CI without separate POMs.

**Profile activation**
- Explicit activation: `-Prelease` on the command line activates the `release` profile; multiple profiles can be active simultaneously with `-Pprofile1,profile2`
- Property-based activation: a profile that activates when `env.CI` is set works identically across GitHub Actions, Jenkins, and GitLab without any pipeline-specific configuration — the CI environment sets the variable automatically
- The `activeByDefault` trap: a profile with `<activeByDefault>true</activeByDefault>` deactivates the moment any other profile is explicitly activated — a developer running `-Prelease` silently disables what they thought was always-on

**What profiles are good for**
- Skipping integration tests locally while running them in CI: the CI profile sets `maven.failsafe.skip=false` and enables JaCoCo; the default profile skips both for developer speed
- Switching Spring active profiles: a CI profile sets `spring.profiles.active=test` via Surefire system properties
- Enabling GPG signing only in the `release` profile — signing on every local build is unnecessary overhead

**The credential security rule**
- Never put credentials in `pom.xml` profiles — Nexus passwords, signing keys, and API tokens belong in `~/.m2/settings.xml`, which lives outside the project directory and is never committed
- In CI, generate `settings.xml` from pipeline secrets using a build step before Maven runs — the URL stays in the POM, the credential stays in the pipeline secret store
- Teams that commit Nexus passwords to pom.xml profiles routinely expose them in public repositories or leak them through repository forks

sections.title: Getting Your Artifact From a Developer Machine to Every Team’s Build — Without Leaking Credentials
sections.content:
Every Java library or shared module eventually needs to be published somewhere other than a developer's laptop. Without a repository manager like Nexus, teams resort to checking JAR files into Git, emailing artifacts, or running `mvn install` on every machine that needs the dependency. This breaks reproducibility — there's no guarantee that the JAR on one machine matches the JAR on another.

**Publishing to Nexus** creates a single source of truth for artifacts. Every developer and CI pipeline resolves dependencies from the same repository, and every version is immutable once released. Maven's `deploy` phase handles the upload by running the entire default lifecycle (compile, test, package) before pushing the artifact to the configured repository.

The process has three pieces: `<distributionManagement>` in the POM declares where artifacts go, `settings.xml` stores the credentials for authentication, and `mvn deploy` executes the upload. Maven automatically routes the artifact to the correct repository based on the version string — a version ending in `-SNAPSHOT` goes to the snapshot repository, while a version without that suffix goes to the release repository. This routing is automatic, which means the same `mvn deploy` command works for both development snapshots and production releases without any configuration change.

sections.title: Configure distributionManagement — The Destination Without the Password
sections.content:
The POM's `<distributionManagement>` block declares both the release and snapshot repository URLs, along with server IDs that act as lookup keys for credentials stored elsewhere. The critical design principle is that **the POM contains the URL but never the password**.

The server IDs must match entries in `settings.xml` — this indirection is what keeps credentials out of version control.

```xml
<distributionManagement>
  <repository>
    <id>nexus-releases</id>
    <url>https://nexus.example.com/repository/maven-releases/</url>
  </repository>
  <snapshotRepository>
    <id>nexus-snapshots</id>
    <url>https://nexus.example.com/repository/maven-snapshots/</url>
  </snapshotRepository>
</distributionManagement>
```

The `<id>` elements are the join key between `pom.xml` and `settings.xml`. When Maven executes `deploy`, it looks up the `<id>` from `<distributionManagement>` in the `<servers>` section of `settings.xml` to find the matching username and password. This design lets the POM be committed publicly while the credentials remain private on each machine or CI runner.

sections.title: Store Credentials in settings.xml — Local for Developers, Injected for CI
sections.content:
Credentials live in `~/.m2/settings.xml`, a file that exists only on the local machine and is never committed to version control. Each `<server>` entry matches a server ID from `<distributionManagement>`.

For CI environments, the credentials are injected as environment variables from pipeline secrets, and `settings.xml` references them dynamically.

```xml
<settings>
  <servers>
    <server>
      <id>nexus-releases</id>
      <username>${env.NEXUS_USERNAME}</username>
      <password>${env.NEXUS_PASSWORD}</password>
    </server>
    <server>
      <id>nexus-snapshots</id>
      <username>${env.NEXUS_USERNAME}</username>
      <password>${env.NEXUS_PASSWORD}</password>
    </server>
  </servers>
</settings>
```

The **`${env.NEXUS_USERNAME}` syntax** reads directly from environment variables, so the actual password never exists in a file on the CI runner. In GitHub Actions, these are stored as repository secrets and exposed to the workflow via `env:` in the YAML. In Jenkins, they come from the credentials store and are injected via the `withMaven` pipeline step.

For local development, developers can store their personal Nexus credentials in `settings.xml` using Maven's password encryption: `mvn --encrypt-password` generates an encrypted token that replaces the plaintext password.

sections.title: Deploy Safely — Especially in Multi-Module Builds
sections.content:
Running `mvn deploy` executes the full default lifecycle — validate through deploy — which means your code is compiled, tested, packaged, and uploaded in one command. Maven determines the target repository automatically: if the version ends in `-SNAPSHOT`, it goes to the snapshot repository; otherwise, it goes to the release repository.

For **multi-module projects**, the default behavior is problematic. Maven deploys each module as soon as it builds. If the third module out of five fails its tests, the first two modules are already published — consumers who resolve dependencies during this window get a **partial build**. The `-DdeployAtEnd=true` flag fixes this by making Maven wait until every module has built and tested successfully before deploying any of them.

```bash
mvn clean deploy -DdeployAtEnd=true
```

This is a non-negotiable flag for multi-module CI pipelines. Without it, a broken build can publish inconsistent artifacts that cause compile failures for every downstream team.

For release management, the **Maven Release Plugin** automates the full workflow: `mvn release:prepare` bumps the version, commits the change, and creates a Git tag. Then `mvn release:perform` checks out the tag, builds the release, and deploys it to Nexus. This ensures the deployed artifact exactly matches the tagged source code — no manual version editing required.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`<distributionManagement>` declares the destination, not the credentials** — the POM specifies release and snapshot repository URLs with server IDs; credentials are stored separately in `~/.m2/settings.xml` to keep them out of version control
- **Server ID is the join key between POM and settings.xml** — Maven matches the `<id>` in `<distributionManagement>` with the `<id>` in `<servers>` to find the correct username and password for authentication
- **SNAPSHOT vs release routing is version-driven** — Maven automatically sends versions ending in `-SNAPSHOT` to the snapshot repository and all other versions to the release repository; no manual switching needed
- **`-DdeployAtEnd=true` prevents partial multi-module deploys** — without this flag, Maven deploys each module as it builds; if a later module fails, consumers resolve an incomplete set of artifacts that break their builds
- **Maven Release Plugin automates version bump, tag, and deploy** — `mvn release:prepare release:perform` handles version editing, Git tagging, building, and deploying in one sequence, ensuring the deployed artifact matches the tagged source exactly

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Publishing to Nexus requires three coordinated pieces: the POM declares where to publish, `settings.xml` holds the credentials, and `mvn deploy` orchestrates the upload. The separation keeps credentials out of version control.

**POM configuration**
- `<distributionManagement>` in the POM specifies both a release repository URL and a snapshot repository URL, each identified by a server ID — the ID is the link Maven uses to look up credentials in `settings.xml`
- Maven routes automatically by version string: if the artifact version ends in `-SNAPSHOT`, it goes to the snapshot repository; anything else goes to releases — the same `mvn deploy` command handles both
- Never put credentials in `<distributionManagement>` — URLs belong in the POM, credentials belong in `settings.xml` under a `<server>` block matching the repository ID

**`settings.xml` and credential management**
- `~/.m2/settings.xml` holds the `<server>` entries with username and password matching the server IDs in the POM — this file lives outside the project directory and is never committed to version control
- In CI pipelines, generate `settings.xml` from pipeline secrets at build time rather than committing it — this keeps credentials out of the repository entirely even in CI configuration
- Use encrypted passwords in `settings.xml` with `mvn --encrypt-password` for additional protection on shared development machines

**Multi-module deploy safety**
- Without `-DdeployAtEnd=true`, Maven deploys each module as it builds — a failure in a later module leaves consumers with a partial, incompatible set of artifacts already published to Nexus
- `-DdeployAtEnd=true` waits until all modules have successfully built before deploying any — either the complete consistent set ships or nothing ships

questions.question: What is the difference between Maven and Gradle?
questions.title: Maven vs Gradle: Key Differences
questions.direct_answer: Maven is an opinionated, XML-based build tool with a fixed lifecycle that favors convention over configuration. Gradle is a flexible, DSL-based build tool with an incremental task graph and a build cache that favors performance and programmability, especially for large or Android projects.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can articulate the trade-offs and choose the right tool for the context.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Dismissing Maven as obsolete — it remains the industry standard for many enterprise Java projects and has excellent tooling support.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss Gradle's remote build cache and configuration cache as qualitative differentiators for large teams, and mention that Gradle can consume Maven POM dependencies and publish Maven-compatible artifacts seamlessly.

sections.title: Convention vs Programmability — What You're Actually Trading
sections.content:
Most comparisons of Maven and Gradle fixate on syntax — XML versus Groovy. But the difference that actually matters in a Java team is what happens when the build runs. Maven processes a fixed sequence of lifecycle phases regardless of whether any work has changed. Gradle constructs a directed acyclic graph of tasks and skips every task whose inputs and outputs have not changed since the last run.

On a project with five modules where you changed one line in one module, Maven rebuilds everything from that module forward. Gradle recompiles only the affected module, pulls unchanged task outputs from cache, and finishes in seconds instead of minutes. This performance gap widens as the project grows — which is why Google chose Gradle for Android and Netflix uses it across hundreds of microservices.

But performance is not the whole story. **Maven's rigidity is also its strength.** Every Maven project looks the same: same directory layout, same lifecycle, same POM structure. A new developer on a Maven project can be productive in an hour. A new developer on a heavily customized Gradle build may need days to understand the build logic. The real decision is not which tool is better — it is which trade-off your team can absorb.

sections.title: Build Model, Performance, and Ecosystem Side by Side
sections.content:
The differences go deeper than syntax and directly affect how your team works day to day.

| Dimension | Maven | Gradle |
|---|---|---|
| Build model | Fixed lifecycle of 23 phases | Directed acyclic graph of tasks |
| Configuration language | XML (`pom.xml`) | Groovy or Kotlin DSL |
| Incremental builds | Re-executes all phases from start | Skips tasks with unchanged inputs/outputs |
| Build cache | None — every CI run starts fresh | Local + remote cache shares results across machines |
| Dependency conflict strategy | Nearest-definition wins (can silently downgrade) | Highest version wins (safer default) |
| Multi-project builds | Reactor builds modules sequentially | Parallel execution with `--parallel` |
| Custom build logic | Requires writing a Maven plugin (Java) | Inline Groovy/Kotlin or convention plugins |
| Learning curve | Low — conventions are explicit | Moderate — DSL requires understanding Gradle's model |
| Ecosystem maturity | 20+ years of enterprise tooling | 12+ years, dominant in Android and modern JVM |

**Neither tool is obsolete.** Maven remains the standard for straightforward Spring Boot services and enterprise codebases where predictability outweighs performance. Dismissing Maven because Gradle is newer ignores the thousands of production systems where Maven's conventions reduce cognitive load and onboarding time to nearly zero.

sections.title: The Decision Framework: Match the Tool to Your Team's Reality
sections.content:
The decision comes down to three questions: how large is the project, how complex is the build logic, and what does the team already know?

**Choose Maven** when your project is a standard Spring Boot service with conventional structure. Maven's fixed lifecycle means fewer decisions during setup, fewer surprises during CI, and easier onboarding. If your team has deep Maven experience and builds finish in under five minutes, switching to Gradle is cost without benefit. The common trap is migrating to Gradle because it is newer, then spending weeks debugging custom build logic that Maven would have handled with a one-line plugin declaration.

**Choose Gradle** when build performance is a genuine bottleneck. If your project has 20+ modules and CI builds take 15 minutes, Gradle's incremental compilation and remote build cache can cut that dramatically. Choose Gradle for Android development where it is the only option, and for polyglot projects mixing Java and Kotlin where the Kotlin DSL provides a consistent build language.

The **practical reality**: Gradle reads Maven POM artifacts and publishes Maven-compatible artifacts. You can migrate one module at a time, measure the improvement, and decide whether to continue. A hybrid organization where some services use Maven and others use Gradle works because both tools share the same artifact ecosystem.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Maven's fixed lifecycle re-runs all phases every time** — `mvn package` always executes validate → compile → test → package even when nothing changed, making builds slower as module count grows
- **Gradle's task graph enables true incremental builds** — each task declares inputs and outputs; unchanged tasks are skipped entirely, and a remote build cache can share compiled outputs across CI and developer machines
- **Nearest-definition vs highest-version conflict resolution** — Maven picks the version at the shallowest depth and can silently downgrade; Gradle defaults to the highest requested version, which is generally safer
- **Custom build logic differs fundamentally** — Maven requires writing a separate Java plugin packaged as a JAR; Gradle allows inline Kotlin or Groovy code in the build script or reusable convention plugins in `buildSrc/`
- **Gradle consumes the Maven ecosystem seamlessly** — Gradle reads Maven POM artifacts from any Maven repository, publishes Maven-compatible artifacts, and imports BOMs via `platform()`, so migration does not require abandoning existing infrastructure

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Maven and Gradle solve the same problem — building, testing, and deploying Java projects — with fundamentally different philosophies. Maven enforces conventions and gives you a predictable lifecycle. Gradle gives you a programmable task graph and dramatically better performance at the cost of a higher learning curve.

**Performance — where Gradle pulls ahead**
- Gradle's incremental build fingerprints task inputs and outputs — tasks whose inputs have not changed are skipped entirely; on a 20-module project this can reduce build time from 15 minutes to under 3 minutes for code-only changes
- The build cache takes this further: Gradle stores task outputs keyed by input hash — a developer machine pulls pre-built outputs from the CI cache instead of recompiling code CI already built
- Maven rebuilds everything from scratch on every run unless you configure specific plugins for incremental compilation; no built-in build cache exists

**When Maven is the better choice**
- For a standard Spring Boot REST API, Maven is often the right call — the Spring parent POM provides sensible defaults, every Java developer understands the lifecycle, and enterprise tooling has decades of Maven-first support
- The migration cost from Maven to Gradle is real — custom build logic that was a plugin declaration in Maven often becomes Groovy or Kotlin DSL code that only the person who wrote it understands
- Teams I have seen struggle with Gradle migrated for the sake of being modern and spent weeks on custom build logic that Maven would have handled declaratively

**Decision criteria**
- Build times under 5 minutes with a team that knows Maven → stay with Maven; the performance gain does not justify the learning cost
- Multi-module projects with complex dependency graphs, Android development, or build times that are a genuine developer productivity bottleneck → Gradle's incremental builds and caching deliver measurable improvement
- New greenfield projects → Gradle with the Kotlin DSL provides type-safe build scripts and better IDE support than Groovy DSL

sections.title: Two Plugins That Replace Hundreds of Lines of Build Configuration
sections.content:
Building a Spring Boot application with Gradle requires exactly two plugins, and getting them wrong is the most common setup mistake. The `org.springframework.boot` plugin adds the `bootJar` task that packages your application as an executable fat JAR with an embedded web server, the `bootRun` task for running locally with hot-reload support, and `bootBuildImage` for creating OCI container images. The `io.spring.dependency-management` plugin imports the Spring Boot BOM — a bill of materials that specifies compatible versions for hundreds of libraries so you never specify version numbers for Spring-managed dependencies.

**The mistake most developers make** is omitting the dependency management plugin entirely. Without it, every dependency declaration needs an explicit version number, and those versions must be manually kept compatible with each other. A Jackson 2.16 with a Spring Web 3.1 that expects Jackson 2.15 produces subtle serialization bugs that only surface at runtime. The dependency management plugin eliminates this entire category of problems by ensuring all managed dependencies resolve to versions Spring has tested together.

sections.title: Apply Plugins and Pin the JDK With a Toolchain
Declare Dependencies Without Version Numbers and Customize the Output
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Two plugins are non-negotiable for Spring Boot** — `org.springframework.boot` provides `bootJar`/`bootRun`/`bootBuildImage` tasks, and `io.spring.dependency-management` imports the BOM so no dependency needs an explicit version number
- **`implementation` replaces Maven's compile scope** — keeps dependencies off consumers' compile classpaths, which means faster compilation and no accidental API leakage when building library modules

sections.title: The Problem: What Breaks When Your Library Leaks Its Internals
sections.content:
Before Gradle introduced the `implementation` and `api` split in version 3.4, every dependency worked like Maven's `compile` scope — visible to everything downstream. If your `service` module depended on Guava internally, every module that depended on `service` could also see and use Guava classes. The moment `service` upgraded Guava or replaced it with a different library, every downstream module broke — even though they had no business using Guava directly.

**This is the dependency leakage problem**, and Gradle's configuration system was redesigned specifically to solve it. The `implementation` configuration makes a dependency available for compilation and runtime within the declaring module, but hides it from any module that depends on yours. The `api` configuration exposes it. The choice between them is not a syntax preference — it determines whether your module's internal dependencies become part of its public contract.

The consequence is practical: a large project using `implementation` everywhere it can compiles faster because Gradle's incremental compiler only reprocesses consumers when the module's public API changes, not when an internal dependency version bumps.

sections.title: Configurations, Conflict Resolution, and the Version Catalog
sections.content:
Gradle organizes dependencies into named **configurations** that map to specific classpaths. `implementation` covers compile and runtime but stays internal. `api` covers compile and runtime and leaks to consumers — use it only in library modules where your public types expose the dependency's types. `runtimeOnly` mirrors Maven's `runtime` scope for things like JDBC drivers.

`compileOnly` mirrors `provided` for annotation processors like Lombok. `testImplementation` and `testRuntimeOnly` cover test-specific needs.

When two dependencies pull different versions of the same library, Gradle resolves conflicts by selecting the **highest requested version** by default. This is safer than Maven's nearest-definition rule, which can silently downgrade a version. For stricter control, `resolutionStrategy.force` pins a specific version, and `strictly` constraints fail the build if any transitive dependency requests a conflicting version.

For managing versions across a multi-module project, version catalogs in `gradle/libs.versions.toml` centralize all coordinates in one file. Every subproject references dependencies as typed accessors like `libs.spring.boot.starter.web`. This replaces the scattered version numbers that drift out of sync when developers copy-paste coordinates between modules. The `platform()` dependency type imports BOMs like Spring Boot's, adopting an entire curated version matrix without declaring individual versions.

sections.title: The implementation vs api Decision in Practice
sections.content:
The distinction between `implementation` and `api` is the single most impactful dependency decision in a Gradle multi-module project. Getting it wrong either leaks internal libraries to consumers or hides types that consumers actually need to compile against.

The rule is straightforward: if a dependency's types appear in your module's public API — in method signatures, return types, or superclass declarations — use `api`. If you only use it internally, use `implementation`. A Spring Boot service module that uses Jackson's `ObjectMapper` internally but only exposes domain objects in its API should declare Jackson as `implementation`, not `api`.

The **compilation speed** impact is measurable. When a module declares a dependency as `implementation` and that dependency's version changes, Gradle only recompiles the declaring module. When it is declared as `api`, Gradle must recompile every module downstream because the dependency is part of the public ABI. On a 30-module project, this difference can turn a 5-second incremental rebuild into a 45-second one.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`implementation` hides dependencies from consumers** — the declaring module can compile and run with it, but downstream modules cannot see it, preventing accidental coupling to internal libraries that may change or be removed
- **`api` exposes dependencies to consumers' compile classpaths** — use only when your public method signatures, return types, or superclass declarations reference the dependency's types directly
- **Highest version wins by default** — unlike Maven's nearest-definition rule which can silently downgrade, Gradle selects the highest requested version, which is generally safer but can still pull breaking major versions
- **Version catalogs in `libs.versions.toml` centralize coordinates** — typed accessors like `libs.spring.boot.starter.web` replace scattered version strings, preventing the drift that happens when developers copy-paste coordinates between modules
- **`platform()` imports BOMs without adding dependencies** — `implementation platform('org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:3.2.0')` adopts Spring's version matrix so individual starters need no explicit version number

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Gradle's dependency management system is built around configurations — named classpaths with specific semantics. The key insight is that `implementation` versus `api` is not just a naming convention; it controls compilation scope and build performance.

**`implementation` vs `api` — the most important distinction**
- `implementation` keeps a dependency internal — downstream modules cannot accidentally import it; changing an `implementation` dependency only recompiles the declaring module
- `api` exposes a dependency publicly — its types appear in the declaring module's public method signatures, and downstream modules can use it; any version change forces recompilation of every downstream module
- The practical rule: default to `implementation` everywhere; switch to `api` only when the compiler tells you a downstream module needs access to the types — overusing `api` defeats the entire configuration system and causes unnecessary recompilation cascades

**Version conflict resolution**
- Gradle's default strategy selects the highest requested version when two dependencies request different versions of the same library — safer than Maven's nearest-definition-wins rule which can silently downgrade
- Version catalogs in `libs.versions.toml` centralize all coordinates in one file — `libs.versions.jackson = "2.16.1"` referenced across all modules ensures consistent versions without duplication
- `resolutionStrategy.force("com.example:library:1.2.3")` pins a specific version regardless of what other dependencies request — use sparingly; it can mask legitimate version conflicts

**Dependency analysis**
- `./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath` shows the full resolved dependency tree for the artifact that ships
- The `com.github.ben-manes.versions` plugin adds `./gradlew dependencyUpdates` which reports which dependencies have newer versions available — useful for regular dependency hygiene

questions.question: What is the Gradle wrapper and why should you use it?
questions.title: The Gradle Wrapper: What It Is and Why to Use It
questions.direct_answer: The Gradle wrapper (`gradlew` / `gradlew.bat`) is a shell script committed to your repository that downloads and runs the exact Gradle version declared in `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`. It ensures every developer and CI machine uses the same Gradle version without requiring a manual installation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the importance of reproducible builds and version pinning in team environments.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running `gradle` directly from a system installation instead of `./gradlew`, which causes builds to break when team members have different Gradle versions installed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention wrapper verification (checking the SHA-256 of the downloaded distribution), using `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 8.5` to upgrade the wrapper, and that CI systems should always invoke `./gradlew`.

sections.title: The 'Works on My Machine' Fix for Build Tooling
sections.content:
Think of the Gradle wrapper as version pinning for the build tool itself. Your `build.gradle` pins Spring Boot to 3.2.0, your `libs.versions.toml` pins Jackson to 2.16.1 — but without the wrapper, the tool that interprets all of these runs at whatever version each developer happened to install last month. One teammate on Gradle 7.6, another on 8.5, CI on 8.3 — and suddenly a build script that should work everywhere fails on one machine because a deprecated API was removed in a newer version.

The **wrapper** is four files committed to your repository: `gradlew` (Unix shell script), `gradlew.bat` (Windows batch script), `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar` (a tiny bootstrap JAR), and `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties` (which declares the exact Gradle distribution URL and optionally its SHA-256 checksum). When you run `./gradlew build`, the shell script checks whether the declared version is cached locally. If not, it downloads it, caches it in `~/.gradle/wrapper/dists/`, and then runs the build. Every developer and every CI agent uses the identical Gradle binary with zero manual installation.

sections.title: Upgrade, Verify, and Enforce the Wrapper Across Your Team
sections.content:
Upgrading the wrapper is a single command: `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 8.6`. This updates `gradle-wrapper.properties` with the new distribution URL. Commit the changed file and every teammate picks up the new version on their next build — no Slack message, no wiki page, no manual download.

For **supply chain security**, add the `distributionSha256Sum` property to `gradle-wrapper.properties`. The wrapper verifies the downloaded ZIP against this checksum before extracting it, catching corrupted downloads or compromised mirrors. On teams subject to compliance audits, this checksum is evidence that the build toolchain has not been tampered with.

The enforcement piece matters most: lint your CI scripts to reject bare `gradle` invocations and only allow `./gradlew`. A single developer running `gradle build` instead of `./gradlew build` can silently use a different Gradle version, produce different outputs, and introduce failures that nobody else can reproduce. Most teams add a CI check that fails if `gradle-wrapper.jar` is missing from the repository or if any pipeline script uses a bare `gradle` command.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Four committed files pin the exact Gradle version** — `gradlew`, `gradlew.bat`, `gradle-wrapper.jar`, and `gradle-wrapper.properties` ensure every developer and CI agent uses identical Gradle binaries with zero manual installation
- **Always invoke `./gradlew`, never bare `gradle`** — running `gradle build` uses whatever version is on `PATH`, reintroducing the exact version inconsistency the wrapper was designed to eliminate
- **`distributionSha256Sum` hardens the supply chain** — the wrapper verifies the downloaded distribution ZIP against this checksum before extracting, catching corrupted or tampered downloads on compromised networks
- **`./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 8.6` upgrades the project** — updates `gradle-wrapper.properties` in one command; commit the change and every teammate picks up the new version automatically on their next build
- **Pre-cache the wrapper in Docker CI images** — bake the Gradle distribution into your CI base image to avoid cold-download latency on every pipeline run, especially behind corporate proxies

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Gradle wrapper solves the build tool version consistency problem — without it, every developer and CI agent runs whatever version of Gradle they have installed locally, and version mismatches cause builds that work on one machine and fail on another.

**What the wrapper does**
- The wrapper commits a shell script (`gradlew`) and a properties file (`gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`) declaring the exact Gradle version the project uses
- Running `./gradlew build` automatically downloads that version if it is not already cached locally — every developer and every CI agent gets the same binary without manual installation
- The wrapper files are small (a few KB) and should be committed to version control — they are the project's contract with the Gradle version

**Security and upgrade**
- Add `distributionSha256Sum` to the properties file to verify the download integrity — without it, a compromised download mirror could substitute a malicious Gradle binary
- Upgrading is a single command: `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 8.6` updates the properties file; commit the change and the entire team and CI pick it up automatically on the next build
- Always call `./gradlew`, never bare `gradle` — add a CI lint step that rejects any pipeline script using the system `gradle` command to prevent accidental version drift in automated environments

**Wrapper in CI**
- CI agents do not need Gradle pre-installed — the wrapper handles it; this simplifies CI image management and ensures every project uses its declared version regardless of what other projects on the same agent use

sections.title: Why a Single build.gradle Becomes Painful at Scale
sections.content:
A Java backend that starts as a single module inevitably grows. The REST controllers, domain logic, persistence layer, and shared utilities all live in one `build.gradle`, one `src/main/java` tree, and one compilation unit. At first this is fine. But once the codebase crosses a few hundred classes, problems compound: changing a repository interface recompiles every controller, test suites run everything on every change, and two developers editing unrelated features create merge conflicts in the same build file.

**A multi-module project** splits the codebase along domain or architectural boundaries. Each module has its own `build.gradle`, its own source tree, and its own dependency declarations. Gradle compiles modules independently and in parallel, so changing the `persistence` module does not trigger recompilation of the `api` module — unless `api` actually depends on `persistence`. The build naturally enforces architectural boundaries that would otherwise be documented but never checked.

The starting point is always `settings.gradle`, which declares which directories are subprojects.

sections.title: Declare Modules in settings.gradle and Wire Dependencies
sections.content:
The `settings.gradle` file is evaluated before any build logic runs. It tells Gradle which directories contain subprojects. Each module listed here must have its own `build.gradle` file.

```groovy
// settings.gradle
rootProject.name = 'order-system'
include 'domain'
include 'persistence'
include 'service'
include 'web'
```

Modules reference each other as `project(':name')` dependencies. Gradle reads these references, builds a dependency graph, and compiles modules in topological order. If `service` depends on `domain`, Gradle compiles `domain` first regardless of declaration order in `settings.gradle`.

```groovy
// service/build.gradle
plugins { id 'java-library' }
dependencies {
    implementation project(':domain')
    implementation project(':persistence')
}
```

The `implementation` keyword means `domain` and `persistence` are internal to `service`. Modules that depend on `service` cannot transitively see `domain` classes unless `service` declares them with `api` instead.

sections.title: Use Convention Plugins Instead of subprojects{} for Shared Configuration
Build Only What Changed With Targeted Task Execution
sections.content:
The primary developer experience advantage of a Gradle multi-module project is targeted execution. Running `./gradlew :service:test` compiles and tests only the `service` module plus any upstream dependencies that need rebuilding. Gradle's incremental build system ensures that if `domain` was already compiled and its sources have not changed, it is skipped.

For CI pipelines, `./gradlew build --parallel` builds independent modules concurrently. On a project with 10 modules where only 3 are in the dependency chain, the remaining 7 build in parallel. The `--build-cache` flag, enabled by default since Gradle 7, restores outputs from previous builds, so clean CI checkouts still benefit from cached compilation.

The key production mistake to avoid is **circular dependencies** between modules. Gradle detects and rejects them immediately, unlike runtime frameworks that might silently tolerate them. Structure modules so that dependencies flow in one direction — domain has no dependencies, persistence depends on domain, service depends on both. This unidirectional flow keeps the dependency graph acyclic and makes build ordering deterministic.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`settings.gradle` declares the project structure** — `include` lists every subproject that Gradle manages; modules not listed are invisible to the build and cannot be referenced as `project(':name')` dependencies
- **Convention plugins replace `subprojects {}`** — define shared Java toolchain, test framework, and linter configuration in `buildSrc/` and apply per-module, so non-Java modules are not forced to inherit JVM plugin settings
- **`project(':name')` dependencies enforce build order** — Gradle resolves inter-module references and compiles in topological order; cycles are detected and rejected immediately, naturally enforcing architectural boundaries
- **Targeted execution saves rebuild time** — `./gradlew :service:test` compiles and tests only the target module and its upstream dependencies, skipping unrelated modules entirely during development
- **`implementation` vs `api` controls module coupling** — declaring `project(':domain')` as `implementation` prevents downstream modules from transitively accessing domain classes through the declaring module's classpath

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A multi-module Gradle project uses `settings.gradle` to define the project structure and convention plugins to share configuration without the brittle `subprojects {}` pattern.

**Project structure and discovery**
- `settings.gradle` includes each subproject with `include(':api', ':service', ':domain')` — Gradle reads this file first and builds the project tree before any build logic runs
- Subprojects reference each other with `dependencies { implementation project(':domain') }` — Gradle builds a dependency graph from these references and compiles in the correct order automatically
- Targeted execution: `./gradlew :service:test` rebuilds only what that module needs — the domain module compiles if it is a dependency, unrelated modules are skipped

**Convention plugins over `subprojects {}`**
- `subprojects {}` in the root build applies settings to every module blindly — a module that needs different behavior requires special-casing with `if (project.name == ...)`, which becomes unmaintainable
- Convention plugins in `buildSrc/` are Kotlin or Groovy files that each module explicitly applies: `apply plugin: 'com.example.java-conventions'` — the module opts in to shared toolchain, test framework, and dependency management configuration
- Different module types apply different convention plugins — an API module applies `java-library-conventions`, a Spring Boot application applies `spring-boot-conventions`; the conventions encode the team's standards once and modules consume them

**When to start with convention plugins**
- Start with convention plugins from day one, not `subprojects {}` — migrating later requires touching every module's build file and is the most common source of inconsistency in multi-module Gradle projects
- Use `dependencyResolutionManagement` in `settings.gradle` for the version catalog — centralizing coordinates there makes them available to all modules without each module importing the catalog separately

questions.question: How does Gradle incremental build work?
questions.title: Gradle Incremental Build: How It Works
questions.direct_answer: Gradle tracks the declared inputs and outputs of every task. Before executing a task it computes fingerprints of those files and properties and compares them to the previous run. If nothing has changed, the task is marked UP-TO-DATE and skipped entirely, saving build time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand how Gradle achieves faster repeated builds and what conditions break incremental behavior.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not annotating custom task inputs and outputs, which means Gradle cannot track changes and always re-runs the task, defeating incremental build.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between up-to-date checks (local, per-task) and the build cache (distributable, shared across machines and CI), and mention that the configuration cache is a separate optimization at the configuration phase level.

sections.title: Why Gradle Rebuilds in Seconds What Takes Minutes From Scratch
sections.content:
Most build tools execute every task on every run. You type `mvn package` and Maven dutifully compiles, tests, and packages even if you changed nothing since the last build. Gradle takes a fundamentally different approach: before executing any task, it checks whether the work has already been done. If a task's inputs and outputs have not changed since the last successful run, Gradle prints `UP-TO-DATE` and skips it entirely.

This is not a simple timestamp check. **Gradle fingerprints every declared input and output** — file contents are hashed, property values are recorded, and the aggregate fingerprint is stored in the project's `.gradle/` directory. On the next build, Gradle recomputes the fingerprints and compares them. A single changed source file in a 500-file module triggers recompilation of that module, but every other module whose inputs are unchanged is skipped in milliseconds.

The mechanism has three layers that build on each other: input/output fingerprinting, the up-to-date check, and the build cache. Understanding each layer explains why Gradle builds get faster over time rather than slower.

sections.title: Input and Output Fingerprinting: How Gradle Knows What Changed
sections.content:
Every Gradle task declares its **inputs** and **outputs** through annotated properties. The `compileJava` task declares source files as `@InputFiles`, the classpath as `@Classpath`, and compiler arguments as `@Input` properties. Its outputs are the compiled `.class` files in the build directory, declared as `@OutputDirectory`. Gradle hashes the content of every input file and records the value of every input property.

After a task executes successfully, Gradle stores these fingerprints in the `.gradle/` directory. Before the next execution, it recomputes the fingerprints and compares them to the stored values. If every input fingerprint matches and every output file still exists with the same content, the task is marked `UP-TO-DATE` and skipped.

The fingerprinting is **content-based, not timestamp-based**. Touching a file without changing its contents does not invalidate the fingerprint. Checking out a branch that has the same source files with different timestamps still produces cache hits. This distinction matters in CI where builds start from a clean checkout — timestamps change on every clone, but content hashes remain stable.

sections.title: The UP-TO-DATE Check: Skipping Work in Milliseconds
sections.content:
When Gradle evaluates a task during execution, it runs the up-to-date check before calling the task's action. The check compares current input fingerprints against stored fingerprints from the last successful execution. If everything matches, Gradle prints the task name with `UP-TO-DATE` and moves to the next task in the graph. No class files are generated, no tests run, no JARs are packaged.

The speed of this check is what makes Gradle's incremental build practical. Computing a content hash of a source file takes microseconds. Comparing stored fingerprints is an in-memory operation. On a 50-module project where you changed one file in one module, Gradle checks and skips 49 modules' `compileJava` tasks in under a second, then recompiles only the changed module.

**Custom tasks participate in this system only if they declare their inputs and outputs.** A task without `@Input` and `@Output` annotations has no fingerprints to compare, so Gradle either always runs it or never detects that it is stale. This is the most common reason teams see `Task :generateConfig EXECUTED` on every build — the task is missing annotations.

sections.title: The Build Cache: Sharing Skipped Work Across Machines
sections.content:
The up-to-date check only works locally — it compares against fingerprints from the last execution on this machine. The **build cache** extends this concept across machines and across time. When a task executes, Gradle stores its outputs in a cache keyed by a hash of all inputs. When any machine encounters a task with the same input hash, it pulls the outputs from the cache instead of re-executing.

The local cache lives in `~/.gradle/caches/`. A remote cache — backed by an HTTP server, Gradle Enterprise, or a cloud bucket — makes this work across the team. A CI build compiles the `domain` module with inputs A and stores the result. A developer who later pulls the same branch has inputs A and retrieves the compiled output from the remote cache in milliseconds instead of compiling locally.

The build cache requires tasks to produce **deterministic outputs**. Timestamps embedded in generated files, random UUIDs in file names, or non-reproducible line ordering break cache hits because the stored output hash would never match a recomputed one. Task authors must use `@CacheableTask` and ensure all outputs are reproducible for cache entries to be reusable.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Content-based hashing, not timestamps** — Gradle fingerprints file contents and property values, so touching a file without changing it or checking out a branch with different timestamps does not invalidate the cache
- **Custom tasks must declare `@Input` and `@Output`** — without annotations Gradle has no fingerprints to compare, so the task either always re-executes or never detects stale outputs, defeating incremental build entirely
- **UP-TO-DATE is local, build cache is distributed** — the up-to-date check compares against the last local execution; the build cache stores outputs keyed by input hashes and serves them to any machine with matching inputs
- **`@CacheableTask` requires deterministic outputs** — timestamps, random UUIDs, or non-reproducible ordering in generated files break cache hits because the stored output hash will never match a recomputed one
- **`--info` diagnoses why a task re-executed** — Gradle logs which specific input or output changed, which is essential for debugging unexpected rebuilds caused by missing annotations or non-deterministic outputs

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Gradle's incremental build is the reason Gradle feels faster than Maven on repeated builds — it treats every task as a pure function and skips re-execution when nothing changed.

**How UP-TO-DATE checking works**
- Before running any task, Gradle hashes all declared inputs — source files, configuration values, classpath entries — and compares the hash to the stored fingerprint from the last successful execution
- If every input hash matches, the task is marked `UP-TO-DATE` and skipped entirely — the output from the previous execution is reused
- Content-based, not timestamp-based: touching a file without changing its content does not trigger a rebuild; this distinction matters in CI where every `git checkout` produces fresh timestamps but identical source files

**The build cache — sharing outputs across machines**
- When a task runs, Gradle stores its outputs keyed by input hash in the build cache — local by default, shared with a remote cache server optionally
- A developer whose input hash matches a task CI already ran pulls the cached output instead of recompiling — a 30-second compile task takes under 200 milliseconds from cache
- Enable remote cache with `buildCache { remote(HttpBuildCache) { url = 'https://your-cache/cache/'; push = System.getenv('CI') != null } }` — only CI pushes to the cache; developers only pull

**Custom task annotation requirements**
- Custom tasks without `@Input` and `@OutputDirectory` annotations on their properties re-execute on every build — Gradle cannot determine what changed if inputs and outputs are not declared
- The symptom: a custom task always shows `EXECUTED` instead of `UP-TO-DATE`; run with `--info` to see which input Gradle detected as changed
- Use `@InputFiles`, `@InputDirectory`, `@OutputFile`, `@Internal` precisely — over-declaring inputs causes false cache misses; under-declaring causes stale output to be used incorrectly

sections.title: The Gauntlet: Why Your First Maven Central Publish Takes Longer Than Writing the Library
sections.content:
Publishing a JAR to Maven Central sounds simple — upload the file and let people download it. In reality, Sonatype's Central Repository imposes a strict set of requirements that most first-time publishers discover one error at a time: a complete POM with license, developer, and SCM metadata; a sources JAR; a Javadoc JAR; GPG signatures on every artifact; and a verified group ID tied to a domain or GitHub organization you control.

**The process flows through three stages.** First, you configure the `maven-publish` and `signing` plugins with all required metadata and GPG key material. Second, you upload artifacts to a staging repository on OSSRH, Sonatype's open-source hosting service. Third, you close and promote the staging repository — Sonatype validates every requirement during the close step, and only after validation passes do artifacts propagate to Maven Central.

Each stage can fail independently, and the error messages are often cryptic. A missing Javadoc JAR causes a close failure with a validation rule name but no clear explanation. Understanding the three-stage pipeline turns a frustrating debugging session into a systematic checklist.

sections.title: Configure the Publication: POM Metadata, Sources, and Javadoc
Sign Every Artifact With GPG and Configure OSSRH Credentials
Upload, Validate, and Promote to Maven Central
sections.content:
The release workflow is a three-step sequence managed by the Nexus publish plugin: upload artifacts to a staging repository, close the staging repository to trigger Sonatype's validation rules, and promote the validated repository so artifacts propagate to Maven Central.

Running `./gradlew publishToSonatype closeSonatypeStagingRepository` executes the first two steps. If validation fails — a missing signature, incomplete POM, or absent Javadoc JAR — the close step throws an error with a link to the Sonatype staging UI where you can inspect exactly which rule failed. Fix the issue and re-run.

For a fully automated release pipeline, `./gradlew publishToSonatype closeAndReleaseSonatypeStagingRepository` adds the promotion step. Artifacts typically appear on Maven Central within 15 to 30 minutes after a successful release.

The **production release workflow** I recommend ties this to Git tags. A CI pipeline triggers on tag push like `v1.0.0`, extracts the version from the tag, sets it in the build, and runs the publish-close-release sequence. This ensures only tagged, reviewed code reaches Maven Central, and the version number is derived from the tag rather than a manual edit in `build.gradle`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Sources and Javadoc JARs are mandatory** — Maven Central rejects any publication missing `-sources.jar` or `-javadoc.jar`; call `java.withSourcesJar()` and `java.withJavadocJar()` in your build script to auto-generate them
- **GPG signatures are required on every artifact** — the `signing` plugin signs the JAR, POM, sources, and Javadoc; use `useInMemoryPgpKeys()` in CI to avoid mounting a GPG keyring on ephemeral runners
- **POM metadata validation happens at staging close** — missing name, description, URL, license, developer, or SCM fields cause the Sonatype close step to fail with rule violation messages, not during upload
- **`io.github.gradle-nexus.publish-plugin` automates the staging lifecycle** — replaces manual OSSRH web UI clicks with a single Gradle task that uploads, closes, validates, and promotes to Maven Central
- **Tie releases to Git tags in CI** — a pipeline that triggers on tag push, derives the version from the tag, and runs the full publish sequence ensures only reviewed, tagged code reaches Maven Central

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Publishing to Maven Central is more involved than publishing to an internal Nexus because Sonatype enforces strict requirements that most internal registries do not — complete POM metadata, sources JAR, Javadoc JAR, and GPG signatures on every artifact.

**The three required plugins**
- `maven-publish` defines the publication and POM metadata — license, developer, SCM URL are all required by Sonatype's validation; a missing field fails the staging close step after upload
- `signing` applies GPG signatures to every artifact; without signatures, Sonatype rejects the staging repository
- `io.github.gradle-nexus.publish-plugin` automates the Sonatype staging workflow: it creates a staging repository, uploads, closes, and releases in sequence without manual Sonatype UI interaction

**Sources and Javadoc — the most commonly missed requirement**
- Call `java.withSourcesJar()` and `java.withJavadocJar()` in the `java {}` block — without these, the upload succeeds but staging close fails because Sonatype's validation rejects the incomplete submission
- Sonatype requires the sources JAR so that IDEs can show source code for library consumers; the Javadoc JAR enables documentation lookup
- The staging close failure message is not always obvious — running with `--info` exposes the exact validation error from Sonatype's API response

**CI release workflow**
- GPG private key and OSSRH credentials must be environment variables in CI — `useInMemoryPgpKeys(findProperty("signingKey"), findProperty("signingPassword"))` reads the key from a property that CI sets from a secret; no GPG keyring needed on the CI runner
- Tie releases to Git tags: pushing `v1.0.0` triggers the CI pipeline that runs the full publish-close-release sequence; no manual steps
- Always publish a snapshot to `https://s01.oss.sonatype.org/content/repositories/snapshots` first to verify the pipeline works before attempting the first production release
